newsitem.title: ITALY: Castro due at Rome food summit dominated by Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Castro due at Rome food summit dominated by Zaire.

text.p: Cuba's veteran communist leader Fidel Castro was due in Rome on Friday to take centre stage at a U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit dominated so far by the mounting tragedy in Zaire.

Airport officials said Castro, who is expected to hold an historic audience at the Vatican with Pope John Paul during his visit to the Italian capital, was due to arrive on a special flight from Havana at around dawn.
Diplomatic sources said the Cuban leader was scheduled to visit the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) in mid-afternoon before talks with Italian officials.

Despite his absence from the opening sessions, the Cuban leader already has a star role as one of six vice-chairmen of the five-day meeting which got under way on Wednesday with a pledge to try to halve global hunger in 20 years.
The summit offers Castro a golden opportunity to blast a 34-year-old U.S. trade embargo and the recent Helms-Burton law designed to squeeze him out of power.
The U.N. General Assembly voted on Tuesday by its biggest majority in five years to lift the ban. Cuba hailed it as a victory for its revolution and proof of Washington's isolation.

A document entitled "Food for All" released by the Cuban delegation on Thursday painted the Caribbean island as a socialist success story despite a U.S. embargo, falling exports and an inability to feed its 11 million people.
But it vowed: "Never, even in the conditions of extreme difficulty which we have been living through in recent years, will we fail our current and future generations."

The document said the Helms-Burton law, which gives Cuban-Americans the right to sue foreign companies that own or operate properties seized by the Cuban government from exiles after the 1959 revolution, had worsened the blockade.
The summit at FAO headquarters has been dominated by Africa and efforts to send an international force into eastern Zaire to help over a million starving Rwandan and Burundian refugees.

"The fate of one million human beings is being played out amid the total indifference of the international community and the governments of the places these people are from," Zaire's Deputy Prime Minister Mutombo Bakafwa Nsenda said.
He said on Thursday that all aid should be sent to Rwanda and Burundi to encourage refugees to go back there.

The situation was sure to be discussed further on Friday but the main debate was on when the world's longest-serving communist leader might meet the Pope, 76, who crusaded against communism in his native Poland and in the Soviet bloc.

The Vatican has made clear it is waiting for Cuba to request an audience, which religious sources said appeared most likely to take place on Saturday because of the Pope's other engagements. It said it had still not received any request.
A meeting between the two men would cement improving relations between Cuba and the Roman Catholic Church and could pave the way for the "Pilgrim Pope" to visit Cuba next year.
"I pray for Cuba every day," the Pope told Cuban exiles on Wednesday staging a "pilgrimage of pain" against alleged human rights abuses under Castro's nearly 38 years in power.
Castro was likely also to come under fresh pressure on the margins of the summit to introduce democratic reforms.

The leaders of Latin American countries and Spain and Portugal sharply criticised Cuba this week. Spain said on Wednesday that it wanted the European Union to join in linking aid to political and economic liberation.
